turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Saturday, the twenty-ninth of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go. [warmly] And it's a weekend, so we get to slow down a little.
[wry] Try to. Three to tease first. The world's most important stretch of sea has been closed for half a year — and this weekend, Iran finally put a price on reopening it.
[curious] Second — bonsai. The art of keeping a tree small for longer than you will be alive. There is a grail tool that is ten per cent better and costs twice as much, and I need to talk about it.
And third: in Japan, the most sober, thrifty young generation in living memory is buying sin by the can. A soda literally called Guilty is outselling everything.
[laughs] Of course it is. Okay — where do we start?
The world. The Strait of Hormuz.
[thoughtful] Set it up for me. How long has it been shut?

About a hundred and eighty days. Roughly six months. That is the longest closure of the strait on record. About a fifth of the world's seaborne oil normally passes through a gap twenty-one miles wide, and since early March it has been effectively closed to routine commercial traffic.
Since Iran's Revolutionary Guard shut it after the February strikes.

Right. What changed this week is not the water — it's the terms above it. On Thursday Iran said it would publish a formal list of conditions to reopen, and until Washington accepts them, the strait stays closed.
So they're not reopening it. They're pricing it.

[deadpan] Exactly. They say they've agreed a safe-transit corridor with Oman — inbound through Iranian waters, outbound through Omani, revenues split. The coordinates are drawn. And not a single commercial convoy has used them.
[skeptical] Drawn but unused. That's not a reopening, that's a billboard.
It's a price tag. And the claim comes from Iranian state media — unverified on the water, which is its own tell.
Where does Washington land?
Flatly the other way. The president said on the eighteenth there are, quote, no talks underway with Iran, and that the strait is already open. Two accounts of the same sea. Both cannot be true.
[curious] What are the two reads on the desk?

Tehran's read is leverage. One deputy foreign minister said the strait cannot be seized by tweet, nor by aircraft carrier. The market's read is gravity — everyone expected oil above two hundred dollars, and China's stockpiling has kept Brent near half that, around eighty-eight.
So the shock the map predicts hasn't landed because Beijing bought a buffer.

And the analysts' warning is that the calm is bought, not structural — the buffer, and the discounts that fund it, run down the longer the lane stays shut. Trackers have it at day one hundred eighty-one — about ten ships a day against a norm of eighty-eight to a hundred and thirty.
[exhales] And the sceptic line? Because 'close to a deal' has a smell to it.

The sceptic line is that a reopening is not near because it keeps being called near. They were close on the fifth of August. The corridor's still unused. A June arrangement already collapsed in July after ships were struck. Watch for one thing: a first convoy that actually sails.
Anything else moving in the world this weekend?

Briefly. A trilateral drill — the United States, South Korea and Japan — off Jeju around the seventh of September, with North Korea promising a corresponding response. The Kremlin confirmed the C.I.A. director's Moscow talks. Nepal's flood toll passed four hundred and seventy, with a barrier lake now dammed by the debris as a second, slower threat. And a fresh seven-and-a-half per cent tariff on China is being scheduled a fortnight before a Xi summit on the twenty-fourth of September.
[wry] The threat and the handshake, booked on the same calendar.
Which is the whole week, really. Speaking of which — the money block. A new Fed chair stepped to the Jackson Hole lectern for the first time.
Kevin Warsh. How'd he do?

[deadpan] He told the market the work isn't done. He said the summer's inflation readings do not show underlying trends meaningfully improving, called two per cent a firm, fixed target, and — pointedly — gave no forward guidance at all. He wants a quieter Fed.
[curious] Quieter meaning less hand-holding.
Less hand-holding. The market heard a hawk. Odds of a September hike, which had drifted down toward thirty per cent, snapped back to the mid-forties.
And the anchors? Gold's been on a tear.

Gold printed a record near four thousand seven hundred and twelve dollars mid-week, then gave back more than a per cent to about four thousand five hundred and forty once Warsh spoke. Bitcoin held roughly flat, near seventy-nine thousand seven hundred. The dollar firmed, the ten-year near four point seven per cent.
[thoughtful] So one force is setting all four.

The price of money, repriced upward. A global-equity tracker rides the risk mood but wears a valuation headwind. Global bonds stay pressured. Gold loses part of its haven bid to a firmer dollar. And the same backdrop caps crypto. Higher-for-longer, tilting to a hike, dollar bid. And that is explanation, Theo — not advice.
[amused] Always the disclaimer. Bring it home to Singapore.
Home is where it gets personal. This is the weekend the cost-of-living help lands — four to six hundred dollars a person, plus two hundred in vouchers — the same month the bills hit a record.
The power tariff.

A record thirty-one point nine one cents a kilowatt-hour. And July's core inflation ticked up to two point zero per cent, not down — driven by electricity and gas up eight point seven on the year. The next tariff revision, due around the thirtieth of September, waits on the very strait we opened with.
[exhales] A chokepoint half a world away, landing on a four-room flat's electricity bill.

Four pages apart in the book, and it's the same story. A study this week found the squeeze now reaches even affluent households. Resale flats slipped a touch, even as a record four hundred and ninety-one sold above a million dollars. Retrenchments hit a five-year high of four thousand five hundred — against a nineteenth straight quarter of job growth.
Mixed, but not weak.
Mixed, but not weak.
[curious] Tech. The biggest company on earth reported.

Nvidia. Ninety-six point two billion dollars in a single quarter — up a hundred and six per cent on the year. Data-centre alone was eighty-nine billion, on the Blackwell ramp. And it guided the next quarter to a hundred and eight billion, assuming zero revenue from China at all.
[excited] A record. And the stock?
[deadpan] Fell.
[laughs] Of course it did.

Priced for perfection. And underneath the record, a quiet move: it's reported to be buying Hugging Face — the hub that hosts the open models the home-lab crowd runs — for about twelve point nine billion. Still unsigned.
[curious] And China? They're still cut off from the top chips, aren't they.

Mostly. Two big Chinese firms are reported to have taken about ten thousand of the step-down chips each — the first real deliveries under the January framework — while the newest Blackwell parts stay barred. The whole hundred-and-eight-billion guide has no China in it, as upside or as cushion. Any policy swing cuts both ways.
So the chipmaker is buying the shelf its models sit on.

The mirror your open weights come from is acquiring a landlord. For the home lab itself, the fun drop was a smaller model — G.L.M. five point three Flash. Three hundred and twenty billion parameters, a permissive licence, a million-token context. The catch isn't the graphics card, it's the memory — about a hundred and seventy gigabytes to run it well.
[wry] Not a laptop model.

Not a laptop model — you need a big unified-memory box, not a gaming card. And there's a twist: the bigger flagship weights were supposed to open the same week and didn't — the lab held them back, citing its own cyber-risk review. Openness versus safety, in miniature. Now — objects. The Kit found a lovely buy-once way into vinyl. Pro-Ject added Bluetooth to its best budget turntable, the E-one-point-two, three hundred and ninety-nine euros.
[skeptical] Bluetooth on a turntable? Isn't that the opposite of the point?
[amused] That's the sceptic line exactly. You're re-digitising an analogue signal to send it wireless. Buy it for the platter and the cartridge — the wireless is a convenience, not a reason.
And the Atelier — the buy-it-once desk. What did we hunt?

Wallets. And here's the thing most people never learn: four ideas — grain, tannage, edge, stitch — let you judge any wallet cold. Full-grain patinas; top-grain cracks; genuine leather is a marketing floor.
[curious] And there's a cult material, isn't there. There's always a cult material.
[warmly] Shell cordovan. It's the dense membrane from a horse's rump. Each hide yields two shells. It takes six to eight months to tan, and it polishes itself to a mirror.
[laughs] A horse's rump. That's the grail.

That's the grail. Ashland Leather in Chicago — run by two men who tan the shell by day and stitch wallets by night — will sell you one for about a hundred and forty-five dollars. And a designer bifold at four hundred is often the same white-label wallet with a logo, marked up thirteen times over.
[amused] And people obsess over which tannery. There's a whole snobbery, isn't there.

[wry] Horween in Chicago, Shinki in Japan, Rocado in Italy — and the forums argue the density of each for pages. One thread is seventy pages of men photographing the patina on their wallets. It is a genuine subculture.
So where's the honest money?
Between ninety and a hundred and fifty dollars. Above two hundred and fifty, you're paying for a name. Below forty, you're buying landfill.
[excited] Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] Bonsai, Claire. Give me the one-sentence version.
Bonsai is not a plant you buy — it's a practice. An ordinary tree, kept miniature and shaped over decades to read as an ancient one. The word is Japanese for planted in a tray.
[curious] And it's a real world? Not three men and a windowsill?
A real world. Roughly an eight-billion-dollar global market, growing near nine per cent a year. The main Reddit forum alone is three hundred and sixty-two thousand people.
Okay — the gear. You promised me a grail tool.

[amused] The tool ladder. A twenty-dollar starter kit gets one line, not a ladder. Then the real stuff: Ryuga, from China, thirty to seventy dollars, where most serious hobbyists live. Then Kaneshin, from Japan, around a hundred and twenty to a hundred and seventy-five.
And the top?
Masakuni. Tokyo, hand-forged. A single pair of shears runs about two hundred and forty-nine dollars.
[gasps] Two hundred and forty-nine dollars for scissors.
[deadpan] And here's the honest part the community says out loud: they're maybe ten to fifteen per cent better than Kaneshin, for a premium over a hundred per cent. Partly it's a flex.
[laughs] I love that they admit it. What else swallows money?

Dirt. There's an imported Japanese clay called akadama that holds water, drains, and deliberately breaks down every season — so you buy it again. A freight shock in twenty twenty-one roughly doubled its price, and it keeps climbing. And the pots are their own collectible world — antique ones run into the thousands.
[amused] A pot worth more than the tree.
Often. Now — the sceptic, because the community is brutally honest here. You will kill your first ten trees.
[chuckles] Encouraging.

The tiny volume of soil punishes every watering mistake. And the real price isn't the money — it's the time. A refined tree is a ten-to-thirty-year project. A specimen can be older than you are. You cannot buy your way to the skill.
[drawn out] Which is kind of the whole appeal, isn't it. And there's a Singapore angle?
A lovely one. Singapore's is a tropical, Chinese-rooted penjing tradition — year-round outdoors — and the local king is a species called water jasmine.
[warmly] Take my hand back out of the rabbit hole. That was a good one.

Quickly through the weekend's culture and the body. The Good Life: Omega refreshed the thirty-eight-millimetre Speedmaster — a Moonwatch face on an everyday automatic, about six thousand five hundred dollars.
The asterisk being?
It looks like the watch that went to the Moon. It is not the watch that went to the Moon. Know which one you're buying.
[laughs] Fair. Screen?

Spider-Man held a fourth weekend, past two point two billion worldwide — a leggy hold, not a surge. And Phoebe Bridgers' new record split the critics from the fans by a hair — universal acclaim, a mild fan quibble about a sixteen-track runtime.
[curious] The family desk — your daughter's age, roughly.

Twelve. Secondary one. And the research keeps saying early adolescence is a sensitive window — habits set hard. The highest-yield move isn't a monitoring app. It's a charging spot outside the bedroom, kept by the adults too.
[warmly] Coach, don't police.

Coach, don't police. And fitness — good news for the time-poor. The longevity data keeps landing on a strength-training sweet spot: about ninety minutes to two hours a week, best paired with cardio. Grinding to six hours doesn't multiply the return.
[warmly] Two hours. I can do two hours.

The honest asterisk is that it's observational — the people who lift are healthier and wealthier to begin with, so some of that is who they are, not what they did. The direction's solid, the decimal points aren't. And a couple for the diary: the Formula One night race in October gets its first-ever Singapore Sprint, Tokyo Game Show turns thirty in September, and there's grand sumo in Kyushu in November. Busan is our weekend deep dive — go in autumn for the film festival, base by the water, and eat the pork-broth soup they do better than Seoul.
[thoughtful] Which leaves the long read. And you buried the lede on this one — the guilty soda.

[drawn out] Japan. The most abstemious generation in the country's modern memory. Around forty-four per cent of people in their twenties never drink. Smoking's near a record low. Many are starving their budgets to feed tax-free investment accounts.
And yet.

And yet the fastest-selling soft drink of the era is a Suntory soda literally named Guilty. Twenty million bottles in the first week. Fifty-five million in fifty days. In a market that had been shrinking.
[curious] Why? What's it actually about?

[drawn out] There's a whole food trend beside it — they call it immoral gourmet, the towering bowl of back-fat ramen. And the surveys are quietly devastating: people eat it alone, feel guilty about half the time, and do it again next week.
So it's not a party. It's a private little sin.

It's a receipt. There's an old idea — the lipstick effect — that when confidence collapses, people buy small, cheap indulgences. Lipstick after a crash. This is that, inverted. Not a cheap way to feel good — a cheap way to feel bad, on purpose.
[warmly] Because when you can't afford the big sins, you buy the small ones retail.

[warmly] Alone, on your lunch break — and you photograph them first. It's the most sin a careful person will let themselves buy. And it's worth watching, because Japan tends to export its moods a few years early.
[exhales] A whole generation, in a two-hundred-yen can.
The records make the headlines. The slow things make the difference.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
